title: Shadowfax Acquires WeFast Assets And Borzo IP For Rs 23.3 Crore
summary: Shadowfax acquires WeFast assets and Borzo IP for Rs 23.3 crore
detailed: Shadowfax Technologies is acquiring WeFast, the Indian business of same-day delivery platform Borzo, for about Rs 23.3 crore ($2.5 million).
The transaction covers India technology, intellectual property, trademarks, customer contracts, equipment, domain names, databases, and employee transfers across multiple agreements.
WeFast operates in over five Indian cities with a network of over 32,000 delivery partners handling more than 1.2 crore deliveries annually.

This matters because the acquisition marks Shadowfax's entry into on-demand intra-city goods transportation, providing an established driver network and customer base without building demand from scratch.
sentences: Listed logistics firm Shadowfax Technologies will acquire WeFast, the Indian business of same-day delivery platform Borzo, for about Rs 23.3 crore, or $2.5 million.
The deal marks the listed logistics company’s entry into on-demand intra-city goods transportation.
Shadowfax has signed agreements to buy the India technology, intellectual property and trademarks of Cyprus-based Incrin.
Owns the Borzo platform, along with the business assets of its Indian arm, WeFast India.

The consideration is split across separate agreements.
Shadowfax pays $2 million to Incrin for India technology, software, intellectual property rights and the BORZO trademark in India.
The rupee equivalent of $50,000 to WeFast India for the WeFast trademark.

A separate agreement covers $450,000 for identified business assets of WeFast India, including customer contracts, equipment, domain names and databases.
That deal also covers a transfer of employees.
At the exchange rate of Rs 93.29 to the dollar used in the filing, the total works out to about Rs 23.3 crore.
WeFast was founded in Mumbai in 2016 and operates in more than five cities.
It has a network of over 32,000 delivery partners and handles more than 1.2 crore deliveries annually, according to Shadowfax.
Through its app, shop owners, distributors and individual consumers can book two-, three- and four-wheelers for urgent deliveries and inventory transfers, with upfront pricing and live tracking.
Shadowfax Technologies built its business on e-commerce shipments, moving parcels from sellers to buyers through a network of partners.
Intra-city on-demand delivery is a different job.
It is booked by a shopkeeper rather than a marketplace, decided in minutes rather than days.
Priced per trip rather than per parcel.
Buying WeFast gives Shadowfax Technologies the customer relationships and the driver network for that business without building the demand side from scratch.
At Rs 23.3 crore, this is a small cheque for a business with 32,000 partners and 1.2 crore deliveries a year.
That price reflects the economics of on-demand logistics, where revenue per trip is low and driver incentives decide contribution margin.
It also reflects the seller’s position.
Borzo’s global business has been restructuring its India operations.
An asset sale at this size is a clean exit rather than a growth transaction.
Shadowfax listed on the stock exchanges earlier this year, which changes how acquisitions are judged.
A listed logistics company buys a smaller rival to add a capability, not to add revenue.
The market will ask what the purchase does for margin per shipment.
Intra-city delivery is also the segment where quick commerce has built its own fleets, so Shadowfax enters a market with well-funded competitors.
Shadowfax has grown through a partner-led model, using third-party riders rather than a full-time fleet.
WeFast’s 32,000 partners fit that model closely, which reduces integration risk on the supply side.
The deal also includes employee transfers, which matters in a delivery business where operations knowledge sits with people rather than systems.
Three things will decide whether this works.
The first is retention of the 32,000 delivery partners.
The network is the asset and partners switch platforms quickly.
The second is whether Shadowfax can price intra-city trips profitably.
Urgent delivery is a convenience product, and customers compare it against a local courier who charges less.
Buying technology, trademarks and employees across three agreements creates handover risk, especially on a platform migration.
